Looking at my land and my situation, I know what I'm going to do — same as I've done for the past thirty years, really. I have about 10 mu of flat ground on the Hebei Plain. The soil is decent loam, though groundwater is getting harder to pump every year. My back isn't what it was, and I can't afford to experiment.

The double-cropping system is the only thing that makes sense here. Winter wheat goes in October, comes off in June. Then I turn around immediately and put in summer maize on the same ground. That's how every family in the village operates. The grain station buys both, the subsidies cover both, and I know how to grow both in my sleep.

For wheat, I'll use the Jimai 22 variety — it's proven here, tolerates the dry springs, and the seed station always has it. I'll rotary-till before planting to work in the base fertilizer. Three irrigations: the winter one to protect the roots from freezing, the jointing irrigation in April which is critical, and one at grain-filling. I spray twice — once for powdery mildew in spring, once for aphids around heading.

For maize, I direct-seed into the wheat stubble right after harvest. No time to till — I need to get the seed in the ground to catch the summer rains. I'll use Zhengdan 958, which is what the seed shop recommends and what my neighbor uses. One irrigation if August is dry, maybe none if the rains come. One pesticide spray for corn borer.

I won't try anything new this year. At 59, my job is to get a stable harvest, pay off the fertilizer loan, and keep going.
